https://www.nps.gov/articles/000/stratot.text: Contact Us Article Stratotype Inventory—John D. Rockefeller, Jr. National Memorial Parkway, Wyoming NPS photo. Introduction John D. Rockefeller, Jr. National Memorial Parkway (JODR), located in Teton County, Wyoming, was authorized by Congress on August 25, 1972 to commemorate Rockefeller’s philanthropy and significant contributions to the establishment of several national parks: GRTE, Acadia National Park (ACAD), Great Smoky Mountains National Park (GRSM), and Virgin Islands National Park (VIIS). Congress also named the highway from GRTE’s south boundary to West Thumb in YELL in honor of Rockefeller ( Anderson 2017 ) . The 132 km (81 mi) parkway encompasses 9,622 hectares (23,777 acres) of remote and largely uninhabited land that provides a natural link between GRTE and YELL (Figure 9). The parkway is a mountainous region with moderate to steep slopes situated between the volcanic plateaus of YELL and the jagged fault-block mountains of GRTE. The geology of the parkway largely reflects influences of extra-regional origin and contains geothermal, glacial, and volcanic features of particular interest (Figures 15 and 16; KellerLynn 2010 ). Jurassic and Cretaceous sandstone and shale are present, but more recent lava and ash from Yellowstone volcanism blanket much of the older Cretaceous bedrock. The most prominent volcanic event was the caldera eruption that created Yellowstone Lake 600,000 years ago, which deposited thick layers of rhyolite in the parkway ( Rodman et al. 1992; KellerLynn 2010 ). The Teton fault, so significant for GRTE, has also uplifted the topography and influenced seismic activity within the parkway. Glaciers originating in YELL entirely covered the parkway during the Pleistocene Epoch (2.6 million to 11,700 years ago), creating its gouged valleys and rounded mountains ( Rodman et al. 1992 ) . Figure 9. NPS park map of GRTE and JODR. NPS image. Significance and Geologic Resource Values The Grand Teton National Park and John D. Rockefeller, Jr. Memorial Parkway Foundation Document ( 2017 ) references the following fundamental resources and values identified for GRTE and JODR: “ Geologic Features and Processes. Powerful ongoing geologic forces shape the park, parkway, and nearby Yellowstone National Park. Regional heat from the earth’s mantle combined with local heat from the plume of magma under Yellowstone have lifted and cracked the earth’s crust. Earthquakes generated along one of these cracks–the Teton fault–tilted the Teton Range skyward while dropping the valley of Jackson Hole. As the mountains were rising, massive glaciers flowed south from Yellowstone and alpine glaciers carved out U-shaped canyons and piedmont lakes ringed by glacial moraines. The glaciers melted, washing soil from the valley floor, and leaving behind an outwash plain covered with cobbles and carving terraces that step down to the modern Snake River. Today, small earthquakes occasionally shake the region, suggesting the power of future mountain-building. Remnant glaciers serve as reminders of the powerful and massive glaciers that shaped the landscape. All the while, rainfall and freeze-thaw cycles cause landslides and rockfalls. ” Figure 15. Bedrock geologic map of JODR, Wyoming. NPS Geologic Resources Inventory base map. Figure 16. Bedrock geologic map legend of JODR, Wyoming. Stratotypes in John D. Rockefeller, Jr. National Memorial Parkway JODR contains one type section and one type area, both of which are associated with Yellowstone volcanism (see Table below; Figure 17). The one type section of JODR is the Pleistocene-age ( Quaternary Period ) Huckleberry Ridge Tuff, the oldest ash-flow sheet of the Yellowstone Group, dating to approximately 2.1 Ma. The Huckleberry Ridge Tuff consists mainly of welded ash-flow tuff that is predominantly devitrified, containing major phenocrysts of quartz, sanidine, and sodic plagioclase with minor phenocrysts of oxides, clinopyroxene, fayalite, zircon, hornblende, allanite, and chevkinite ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). Christiansen and Blank ( 1972 ) designated the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff type section as the cliff exposure at the head of a large landslide 1.8 km (1.1 mi) N10° E of the Snake River bridge at Flagg Ranch along the John D. Rockefeller highway about 3 km (2 mi) south of the South Entrance of YELL (Figure 17). The type section is approximately 170 m (560 ft) thick and consists of welded phenocryst-rich rhyolitic ash-flow tuff overlying Cretaceous sandstones and shales (Figure 18; Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). Modified geologic map of JODR showing stratotype locations. The transparency of geologic units has been increased. NPS Geologic Resources Inventory base map. Figure 18. Basal fallout ash of Huckleberry Ridge Tuff, Mount Everts, YELL. A: continuous planar bedding of fallout tuff; lower, lighter colored part is relatively fine-grained, darker upper part is coarser grained. B: fused tuff at top of basal fallout, overlain by vitrophyric welded ash-flow tuff. Figure from Christiansen (2001). Ash flows of the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff type section are divided into three members due to significant changes in welding and minor variations in phenocryst content ( Christiansen 1979; Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). The oldest member (A) is approximately 45 m (150 ft) thick and contains abundant (40–50%) phenocrysts at its base that become less abundant in the upper 15 m (50 ft). The middle member (B) is approximately 30 m (100 ft) thick and has a thin, phenocryst-poor base with a zone of abundant large phenocrysts above it ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). The top of member B contains distinct dark crystallized pumice that is overlain sharply by member C ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). Member C is approximately 95 m (310 ft) thick and is characterized by smaller, moderately abundant phenocrysts than the other underlying members ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). The one geologic type area of JODR is for the Pleistocene-age Lewis Canyon Rhyolite. Stratigraphically, the Lewis Canyon Rhyolite overlies the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff and consists of several bulbous, non-stratiform rhyolitic lava flows dated to approximately 0.85 Ma (850,000 years ago) ( Christiansen and Blank 1972; Christiansen 2001 ). The rhyolite is characterized as containing 30–40% phenocrysts, including abundant sodic oligoclase with smaller, less abundant phenocrysts of quartz, sanidine, clinopyroxene, and opaque oxides ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). Christiansen and Blank ( 1972 ) designated the type area as the north side of Glade Creek, between the Snake River and the east end of Grassy Lake Reservoir (Figure 17). In this area the Lewis Canyon Rhyolite is represented by well-exposed, 200 m (660 ft) thick flows that occur along the meadows on the north side of Glade Creek. The type area rhyolite overlies the Huckleberry Ridge Tuff and Cretaceous sedimentary rocks and is overlain by the Lava Creek Tuff ( Christiansen and Blank 1972 ). Leave No Trace—Protect Type Sections for Science Many type sections and paleontological sites are vunerable to damage from careless visitation and over-use. Be sure to practice Leave No Trace princples whenever you are in the outdoors. Of particular importance at geoheritage sites is to: Travel and camp on durable surfaces, and Leave what you find. If you see signs of vandalism or someone acting inappropriately during your visit to a park site, please contact a ranger at the park or make a report through NPS Investigative Services . https://www.nps.gov/articles/marquette.h.text: Contact Us Michigan: Father Marquette National Memorial Visitor Center at Father Marquette National Memorial Straits State Park, Michigan Department of Natural Resources and Environment The 1600s and 1700s were an age of discovery in North America. While American Indian tribes had a great knowledge of the land, for representatives of the European colonizing nations it was a new frontier. France was one of the earliest European nations to explore what is today Canada and the northern United States, establishing its colony of New France. Father Jacques Marquette was among the leading French explorers in the New World. On behalf of France, Father Marquette and Louis Jolliet explored and mapped the Mississippi Valley, documenting its rivers and peoples. Today, visitors to Father Marquette National Memorial in St. Ignace, Michigan can learn about the life of this remarkable priest and traveler. Born in France in 1637, Jacques Marquette became a missionary in the 1650s. In 1666, he was sent to Quebec, one of the major settlements in New France. At its height, New France covered a vast area ranging roughly from Newfoundland and the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico. Between his arrival in Quebec and 1669, Father Marquette traveled throughout New France, mostly in what is today the northern United States and southern Canada, spending time with various Indian tribes learning tribal languages. When he died, he spoke six tribal languages. From Quebec he went briefly to assist as a missionary in Sault Ste. Marie. Marquette soon left Sault Ste. Marie to found his own mission. In 1671, Marquette established a community ministering to French fur traders and native populations around eastern Lake Michigan. Originally located on Mackinac Island, Michigan, the mission relocated to St. Ignace, Michigan. Marquette did not remain long in St. Ignace as larger forces of empire intersected with his life. Though Marquette may have come to North America to preach and convert, he was very much part of a different kind of conquest. As a colonizing power, France had an interest in exploring the central regions of the present-day United States. Less than a year after arriving in St. Ignace, Father Marquette joined an expedition to map and document this unknown region. Louis Jolliet, a native of New France, led the expedition. In 1672, Jolliet and Marquette, chaplain on the trip, traveled from Michigan to Louisiana and then back up north, exploring the area that is near the City of Chicago today. The group traveled south on the Mississippi River, turning around where the Arkansas River joins the Mississippi. Though the Jolliet-Marquette expedition could have continued even further south, the expedition halted here to avoid another colonizing power--the Spanish. Much as the French were beginning to explore and spread in the north, so were the Spanish in the south. To avoid a confrontation, the Jolliet-Marquette group returned north via the Mississippi and Illinois rivers and Lake Michigan. Though the accomplishment of journeying almost the length of the United States in canoes alone is significant, the Jolliet-Marquette expedition is important for other reasons. Much of Jolliet’s notes suffered damage during the trip, leaving those of Marquette as the primary record of this amazing journey. Marquette’s notes established that settlement of the interior of New France was possible. A strong river, the Mississippi, ran from the north to the south, providing access and easily farmable land deep within French holdings. Though New France never expanded to fill the areas visited by Marquette and Jolliet, records of their expedition were invaluable to later explorers, and historians have found Marquette’s notes on the various American Indian groups useful. Some of these later explorers established Arkansas Post, which is also included in this travel itinerary. Father Marquette died in 1675 in present-day Ludington, Michigan. Although he was originally buried there, his followers moved his body to the chapel of the mission he established at St. Ignace. This mission is located at State and Marquette streets. Today, visitors to Father Marquette National Memorial can learn more about Marquette by viewing the memorial and walking an outdoor trail that includes signs with information about the life of this great French explorer. Father Marquette National Memorial is located in St. Ignace, MI, west of Interstate 75, off US Route 2. The memorial is within Straits State Park operated by the State of Michigan. Father Marquette National Memorial is also included as part of the North Country National Scenic Trail . You Might Also Like Loading results... https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/b.text: Contact Us Barrys Island Trail Barry's Island Hiking Trail. Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Barry’s Island Trail: Moderate, 4 Miles Round Trip The Barry’s Island trail starts as a two-track road leading north from the Barry’s Landing parking lot. The trail goes around Chain Canyon, a secret escape route for cattle rustlers in the late 1800s and early 1900s. At Barry’s Island, the road to the west goes to Medicine Creek Campground, a boat-in or hike-in only campground. Continue following the road northeast (clockwise) around the island. The variation in water elevation is evident. During years of high water, the trail can be covered. If that is the case, take the bypass trail above the main trail. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/b.text: Contact Us Beaver Pond Nature Trail Beaver Pond Trail in Winter. NPS Beaver Pond NatureTrail: Moderate, 2.6 Mile Round Trip Begin hiking at the west end of the sidewalk at the Afterbay Contact Station . Travel across the yucca flats to the ridge above Lime Kiln Creek. Below, the creek is covered with gnawed trees and other building materials. This is one construction site you will want to take a closer look at. The trail begins to wind down the steep hillside to the bottom, where you can sit among the beaver ponds and marvel at these creatures’ ingenuity. If you are looking for a longer hike, cross the bridge and make your way along the opposite plateau. The views of the Afterbay are yours alone to enjoy. The trail continues to the service road. You come to a “T” in the road. Take the right to end your hike at the Afterbay Campground for a total of 1.3 miles each way. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/b.text: Contact Us Bighorn Head Gate Trail The end of Bighorn Head Gate Trail in the winter. NPS Head Gate Trail: Easy, 0.1 Mile Round Trip Drive through the Afterbay Campground past the sign that says “No Camping Beyond this Point,” to the pit toilet at the end of the road. From here a short hike down a gravel path takes you to a quiet area near what remains of the Bighorn Head Gate . The Bighorn Head Gate was part of the original irrigation system used in the upper Bighorn Valley in the early 1900’s before the dam was built in 1965. The best time of year to view the head gate is during the winter since most of the head gate is underwater during the summer months. This is a great place for bird watching. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/h.text: Contact Us Hillsboro Trail Hillsboro Hiking Trail. Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Hillsboro: Easy to Moderate, 1 to 3 Miles Round Trip Attracted to the colors of the canyon and the possibility of those colors yielding gold, Dr. Barry began exploring Bighorn Canyon in the 1890s. During his exploration, he happened upon the Trail Creek Valley. He never found enough gold to make himself rich, but the canyon and the surrounding environment offered all he needed to make another kind of fortune. He converted to operating a guest ranch. He used the natural opportunities of hiking, fishing, hunting, camping, and horseback riding to entice more clientele to his ranch. You may visit Hillsboro in the Trail Creek Valley one of two ways: the first, a one-mile round trip hike begins by driving up the red dirt road between Trail Creek campground and Barry’s Landing to a closed gate. From there, a half-mile hike will take you to the abandoned site of Hillsboro ranch . Take some time to explore the buildings and learn how the Barrys ran the Hillsboro Guest Ranch . Don’t forget to stop at the corrals below the kiosk on your way back. The second option is a three-mile loop. You may start either in the campground or at the gate and walk to the ranch. The trail continues behind Eddy Hulbert ’s cabin on the historic ranch road up to the park road. Follow the road to the Barry’s Landing turnoff back to where you began. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/l.text: Contact Us Lockhart Ranch Trail Lockhart Ranch Hiking Trail. Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Lockhart Ranch: Easy, 0.5 or 2.1 Miles Round Trip Beyond the Barry’s Landing junction, the park road becomes unpaved. Follow this dirt road to the trailhead. The Lockhart Ranch is representative of life for western ranchers in the late 19 th and early 20 th centuries. The gentle flow of Davis and Cottonwood Creeks provided the life force of the ranch. Ditches running from Davis Creek took advantage of the natural topography of the land by using gravity to irrigate the surrounding pastures. You can take the half-mile loop through the ranch or you can take an extended two-mile hike along the historic county road. The trail begins at the two-track road east of the corrals near the garage. Follow the road along the northern edge of Caroline Lockhart ’s livestock pastures. This path leads to Davis Creek. Following the two-track along Davis Creek will bring you to an old metal gate and the dirt road. Instead of going through the gate, follow the inside of the fence to the crossing at Davis Creek. Continue following cowpaths along the inside of the fence over the hill to a corner post. Seven fence posts south of the corner post a faint two-track turns southeast. Follow the two-track to loop back to the ranch. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/l.text: Contact Us Lower Layout Creek Trail Lower Layout Trail in Spring Photo by Ben Goodlad Lower Layout Creek Trail: Easy to Moderate, 3.4 Miles Round Trip The Lower Layout Creek trailhead is located at the cattle guard that marks the northern end of the Pryor Mountain Wild Horse Range . At the cattle guard, park on either side of the road making sure you are not blocking the flow of traffic. The trail begins by hiking the old two-track road south of Layout Creek. There are several opportunities to stray from the main trail to view Layout Creek Canyon as well as see the bighorn sheep and horses that use the area. The trail forks a short distance from Bighorn Canyon. Continue following the trail to the right to the bottom of the plateau. A well-trodden horse trail leads to the top of the plateau and another amazing view. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/m.text: Contact Us Mouth of the Canyon Trail Mouth of the Canyon Trail Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Mouth of the Canyon Trail: Moderate, 1.8 Miles Round Trip Seldom-seen views of the canyon, as well as spectacular views of the Pryor and the Bighorn Mountains, can be seen from this trail. The deep red Chugwater outcrops are a sharp contrast to the surrounding geologic colors of Bighorn Canyon. To explore the colors and contrasting scenery Horseshoe Bend has to offer, begin hiking at the service road on the north end of loop B in Horseshoe Bend Campground near campsite number B-15. Just before reaching the water storage tank, veer right onto an abandoned two-track. Follow the two-track up and around the hills toward the canyon. When the road disappears, follow the trail markers along the Pryor Mountain Wild Horse Range boundary fence. From this vantage point, you can see the mouth of the canyon and its union with Crooked Creek. This colorful setting invites one to rest and watch the horses graze below and the birds soar above. You may either go back the way you came along the abandoned two-track road or follow the trail through a juniper-lined draw to the top of the ridge and back to the road. Please stay on the trail to help preserve the cryptobiotic soil. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/r.text: Contact Us Rangers Delight Trail Ranger's Delight Trail in the summer Photo by Ben Goodlad Ranger Delight: Easy to Moderate, 0.66 Miles Round Trip Park in the designated area on the west side of the park road one-half mile north of the Montana state line. The trail begins on the east side of the road on the lower north edge of the draw. While following the faint road cut, it is easy to feel like the only person that has ever hiked this trail. Continue to follow the trail through the saddle and toward the canyon. At the cut-off fence post and trail marker, you can turn left and hike toward the rim. This is the end of the trail. Walking to the right will bring you into the bend of the river and give unique views of the canyon. Walking to the left, you have a good view of the ledge below with a sheep trail that treacherously traces the canyon rim. For more solitude and exploration go back to the cut-off fence post and continue to follow the road cut and trail markers to the State Line trail. The connecting trail is 0.37 miles each way. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/s.text: Contact Us Sykes Mountain Trail Sykes Mountain Trail in the summer. Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Sykes Mountain Trail: Hard, 4.6 Miles Round Trip with 1,250 feet elevation gain Sykes Mountain Trail is a rugged hike up a desert mountain that directs the hardy hiker to overlooks of Bighorn Canyon and Horseshoe Bend. This is a favorite hike for many but is less enjoyable during hot summer days. The trail begins at the Horseshoe Bend access road sign. You may park in the Ranger Station parking area across the road. Follow the trail markers around the hill and into the first drainage until you see a small game trail. At the rockslide, cross to the east side of the drainage. Here the game trail disappears. Continue to follow the trail markers, making your way upward. At the top, a deep canyon forces you to go east. Follow the ridge to where it begins to bend into a horseshoe. From here follow the trail markers through the shallow drainage to the overlook. There are two hills southwest of the overlook. The taller of the two is called Crooked Creek Summit. For a longer hike cross the juniper flats and proceed to the summit. From here you can see vistas of surrounding landscapes and the mountains that enclose the Bighorn Basin. NPS Three Mile Access Trail: Easy, 2 Miles Round Trip At the west end of the Three Mile Parking Area, near the pit toilet, follow the gravel path along the Bighorn River. Travel along the well-trodden footpath skirting the field along the river. The trail ends in a grove of cottonwoods with giant downed logs perfect for watching the graceful casting of the fly fishermen that come from all over to enjoy the world class fishery supported by the Bighorn River. It is also a tranquil setting to watch the ducks floating by or just listen to the sounds of nature. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/t.text: Contact Us Two Eagles Interpretive Trail Two Eagles Interpretive Trail NPS Two Eagles Interpretive Trail: Easy, Handicapped accessible, 0.25 Miles Round Trip The site has been used by Native Americans for over 10,000 years. In the vicinity of the trail there are more than 140 stone circles. The stones were used by tribal families to hold down the edges of tipis. When they moved to their next encampment, they would simply roll the stones off and leave the rocks in place for their next visit. This is a historic site of cultural interest. The stones need to be left in place for future generations to enjoy and learn from this rich history. https://www.nps.gov/bica/planyourvisit/u.text: Contact Us Upper Layout Creek Trail Upper Layout Creek Trail in the summer Photo by AIRs Diane Durant & Devyn Gaudet Upper Layout Creek Trail: Hard, 1.8 Miles Round Trip 1250 feet elevation gain Erastus T. Ewing came to Bighorn Canyon looking for gold. Finding none he decided to try his hand at ranching. He knew that to make it in this arid land he would need water. In 1897, he filed to appropriate 200 inches of water per year from Layout Creek for irrigation, mining, and milling. In passing years, other inhabitants built holding ponds and added more ditch systems From the park road, immediately beyond the Pryor Mountain Wild Horse Range boundary, a historic site marker directs you to the Ewing/Snell Ranch . The Upper Layout Creek trail begins in the parking area to the right of the corrals. You may begin hiking here or drive to the end of the gravel road. The road ends in a small parking area big enough for two cars and the trail begins, following trail markers down to Layout Creek. The trail winds up Layout Creek Canyon past the waterfall to Layout Creek Springs. This lush secluded canyon offers a striking contrast to the surrounding arid plateau and emphasizes the importance of water to the land. There is a concrete loop around the pond, which offers a great place to see red-winged blackbirds and boreal chorus frogs during the summer. The pond was originally built to reflect light on solar panels that have long since been removed from the building. The pond is now slowly being reclaimed by nature and will one day become a small marshland. Board of Education National Historical Park Kansas  September 2025 Mission of the National Park Service The National Park Service (NPS) preserves unimpaired the natural and cultural resources and values of the national park system for the enjoyment, education, and inspiration of this and future generations. The National Park Service cooperates with partners to extend the benefits of natural and cultural resource conservation and outdoor recreation throughout this country and the world. The NPS core values are a framework in which the National Park Service accomplishes its mission. They express the manner in which, both individually and collectively, the National Park Service pursues its mission. The NPS core values are: · Integrity: We deal honestly, ethically, and fairly with the public and one another. · Stewardship: We provide and inspire exceptional care of the places entrusted to us by the American people. · Respect: We embrace our differences and treat each person with dignity. · Engagement: We each participate fully and extend genuine invitations to all. · Collaboration: We succeed by engaging beyond our silos, tapping new ideas, and expanding our community. · Accountability: We earn the public’s trust each day by competently and transparently fulfilling our responsibilities. The National Park Service is a bureau within the Department of the Interior. While numerous national park system units were created prior to 1916, it was not until August 25, 1916, that President Woodrow Wilson signed the National Park Service Organic Act formally establishing the National Park Service. The national park system comprises more than 400 park units covering more than 84 million acres in every state, the District of Columbia, American Samoa, Guam, Puerto Rico, and the Virgin Islands. These units include, but are not limited to, national parks, monuments, battlefields, military parks, historical parks, historic sites, lakeshores, seashores, recreation areas, scenic rivers and trails, and the White House. The variety and diversity of park units across the nation require a strong commitment to resource stewardship and management to ensure both the protection and enjoyment of these resources for future generations. Introduction Every unit of the national park system will have a foundational document to provide basic guidance for planning and management decisions—a foundation for planning and management. The core components of a foundation document include a brief description of the park as well as the park’s purpose, significance, fundamental resources and values, other important resources and values, and interpretive themes. The foundation document also includes special mandates from the park’s enabling legislation or other legislation that impacts park management and resource protection. A primary benefit of developing a foundation document is identifying and clearly stating in one document the essential information that is necessary for park management to consider when determining future planning efforts, outlining key planning issues, and protecting resources and values that are integral to park purpose and identity. A foundation document aids park managers, staff, park partners, and the public in understanding a unit of the national park system. Brief Description of the Park Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park is co-located in Topeka, Kansas, and Summerton, South Carolina. The park includes the historic Monroe Elementary School in Topeka and the historic Scott’s Branch High School and Summerton High School in Summerton. All three schools are located in neighborhoods that include residences, light industries, small businesses, and vacant lots. Topeka, the Kansas state capital, is a city of approximately 125,000 people in the eastern plains along the Kansas River. Summerton is a small town in Clarendon County, South Carolina, with a population of approximately 800 people. Brown v. Board of Education National Historic Site was established by Public Law 102-525 in Topeka, Kansas, on October 26, 1992. The site later opened to the public in 2004 on the 50th anniversary of the Brown v. Board of Education ruling. On May 12, 2022, Public Law 117-123 renamed the site as a national historical park and expanded it to include two additional sites in Summerton, South Carolina. Monroe Elementary School and Sumner Elementary School had been designated a national historic landmark in 1991, while Summerton High School was listed in the National Register of Historic Places in 1994, and Scott’s Branch High School was listed in 2023. The park interprets the people, places, and events that contributed to the landmark US Supreme Court decisions that declared racial segregation in public education unconstitutional. Furthermore, the park interprets the integral role of the cases that the court combined in the Brown v. Board of Education decision in the context of the civil rights movement. In expanding the park in 2022, the law added to the purpose “to honor the civil rights stories of struggle, perseverance, and activism in the pursuit of education equity.” Working with partners enriches the services provided by the park staff and allows educators and NPS rangers to reach new, untapped audiences. The US Supreme Court decision in Brown v. Board of Education is one of the most pivotal opinions ever rendered by that body. On May 17, 1954, at 12:52 p.m., the Court issued a unanimous decision stating that it was a violation of the 14th Amendment to separate children in public schools for no reason other than their race. Since the case from DC could not rely on the protections of the 14th Amendment, the court issued a similar opinion that relied on the protections of the 5th Amendment, which did apply to DC. This landmark decision highlights the court’s role in affecting changes in national and social policy. Often when people think of the case, they remember a little girl whose parents sued so that she could attend an all-White school in her neighborhood. However, the story of Brown v. Board of Education is far more complex. In the middle third of the 20th century, the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) and other civil rights organizations were actively at work filing cases that challenged racial discrimination in an array of areas including voting, public transportation, teacher salaries, and higher education. The NAACP Legal Defense Fund determined public education the most viable pathway to end legal segregation because of its role in promoting an equal society, and in the 1930s, they developed a legal strategy to challenge segregation in schools. As the Cold War ideologies of the Soviet Union and the United States emerged as global counterpoints, the practice of racial segregation became an international issue rather than just a domestic one. As the US sought new allies to counter Soviet gains in Eastern Europe, the country was forced to recognize its inconsistency of advocating for freedom and equality on the international stage while denying basic rights to its African American citizens at home. President Harry S Truman established the President’s Committee on Civil Rights in 1946. A year later, he used executive authority to order desegregation of the military, a direct response to the brutal blinding of WWII soldier Isaac Woodard in Batesburg, South Carolina. In 1948, the committee issued its report To Secure These Rights, which called for “the prohibition of segregation in the public school system of the District of Columbia” among its recommendations. The Supreme Court declared unconstitutional the racially restrictive covenants that prevented African Americans and other minority groups from purchasing property in White neighborhoods. Additionally, the NAACP won numerous legal victories to integrate colleges in Oklahoma, Texas, and Missouri that established a new legal precedent to challenge segregation in public schools. After nearly 60 years of “separate but equal,” a precedent set in Plessy v. Ferguson in 1896, the NAACP and the nation were on the verge of a major victory against segregation. In South Carolina during 1947, a parent from rural Summerton began a petition requesting that Black students be provided the same bus transportation available to White students. Prior to the petition, the Clarendon County school board reserved all the buses in its fleet for White children, leaving Black students as much as a nine mile walk to school. To aid this effort, parents retained attorneys Harold Boulware and Thurgood Marshall. Marshall’s opinion was that the bus transportation inequity violated “separate but equal” and used that strategy moving forward. In late summer of 1948, members of the Topeka chapter of the NAACP volunteered to challenge the “separate but equal” doctrine governing public education. NAACP Topeka Branch President McKinley Burnett continued to petition the Board of Education to voluntarily desegregate the public schools while branch lawyers began assembling a case and signing up plaintiffs, often recruiting friends and neighbors. A group of parents agreed to participate on behalf of their children. In 1949, after the rejection of Pearson v. Clarendon County, NAACP attorneys switched tactics and reached beyond their case for equal bussing. They asked fot full equal educational opportunities for students in Clarendon County. Leaders in the community worked together with parents to garner enough signatures on the “Equal Everything” petition to sue in federal court, calling for “educational advantages and facilities equal in all respects to that which is provided for whites.” As news of the petition reached the larger community, signers began to face backlash in the form of job loss, evictions, and violence. The year 1950 brought continued struggle. In May, Briggs v. Elliott was officially filed in federal court. That summer, the NAACP Topeka branch secretary notified the NAACP in New York that, in her words, the school situation had grown unbearable, and they were prepared to go to court. In early 1951, Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka, Kansas was filed in the US District Court for Kansas. To make the case that separate could not be equal, the legal team relied on the work of social scientists who had been studying the effects of segregation on Black children. In preparation for the Briggs v. Elliott case, Marshall asked Dr. Kenneth Clark to repeat experiments with school children from Scott’s Branch using light- and dark-skinned dolls. Clark asserted that his tests showed the psychological damage on Black children caused by prejudice and segregation. He and other social scientists testified that segregation gave African American children a sense of inferiority. In December 1952, the US Supreme Court had on its docket cases from Kansas (Brown v. Board of Education), Delaware (Gebhart v. Belton), the District of Columbia (Bolling v. Sharpe), South Carolina (Briggs v. Elliott), and Virginia (Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County), all of which challenged the constitutionality of racial segregation in public schools. The US Supreme Court consolidated these five cases under one name, Oliver Brown et al. v. the Board of Education of Topeka. One of the justices later explained that the court felt it was better to have representative cases from different parts of the country. There is no definitive explanation for why the court chose to list the Topeka case first. Years after the decision, Justice Tom Clark related that they had decided to put Brown first “so that the whole question would not smack of being a purely Southern one.” This collection of cases was the culmination of years of legal groundwork laid by the NAACP in its work to end segregation. None of the cases would have been possible without the many individuals who were courageous enough to challenge segregation in public-school systems. Each of the five cases that collectively formed Brown v. Board of Education at the Supreme Court level varied in their specifics. The lack of school buses, educational facilities, and basic supplies were among the evidence in the cases outside of Kansas. In Topeka, the African American schools were housed in quality buildings with supplies and teacher pay commensurate with the city’s White schools. However, children of the plaintiffs were denied access to the schools much closer to their neighborhoods. They had to attend more distant facilities designated for their race. Persuaded by the expert testimony of social scientists, Chief Justice Earl Warren related the court’s unanimous opinion that the legal separation of Black children gave them “a feeling of inferiority as to their status in the community that may affect their hearts and minds in a way unlikely to ever be undone.” Legal scholars note that the Brown v. Board of Education decision was the first in which the Supreme Court used sociological research in crafting its ruling. The court firmly rejected the precedent of Plessy v. Ferguson that had created the doctrine of “separate but equal.” The court declared “that in the field of public education the doctrine of ‘separate but equal’ has no place. Separate educational facilities are inherently unequal.” Following the landmark Brown v. Board of Education decision, resistance to school integration quickly spread across the nation, determined to make integration as difficult as possible. In 1955, the Supreme Court issued another opinion, commonly called Brown II, in which it ordered federal courts to oversee public school integration “with all deliberate speed.” In South Carolina, the state had attempted to circumvent the expected Brown ruling by developing “equalization schools” (the first being Scott’s Branch in Summerton) and after the ruling, the state immediately made plans to appeal. The state announced in 1954 that it would end aid to any school accepting Black students as transfers. Ku Klux Klan activity increased with planned attacks on local participants of the case. By August of 1955, Clarendon County officials told Marshall that they would close schools rather than integrate them. It was not until 1965 that Black students were enrolled at the previously all-White Summerton High School. The experience in South Carolina echoed across the southern United States as communities grappled with the real-life impact of the Brown decision and developed strategies collectively known as massive resistance. Court battles continued for decades after the decision, and communities across the country adopted many strategies—some more successful than others—to achieve education equity in the US. Park Purpose The purpose statement identifies the specific reason(s) for establishment of a particular park. The purpose statement for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park was drafted through an analysis of its enabling legislation and the legislative history that influenced its development. The park was established when the enabling legislation adopted by Congress was signed into law on October 26, 1992, and redesignated and expanded by further legislation on May 12, 2022 (see appendix A for enabling legislation and subsequent amendments). The purpose statement lays the foundation for understanding what is most important about the park. The purpose of Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park is to preserve, protect, and interpret the resources related to the landmark US Supreme Court decisions that declared unconstitutional the racial segregation of children in public schools; to interpret the integral role of the Brown v. Board of Education decisions in the civil rights movement; and to honor the civil rights stories of struggle, perseverance, and activism in the pursuit of education equity. Park Significance Significance statements express why a park’s resources and values are important enough to merit designation as a unit of the national park system. These statements are linked to the purpose of Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park, and are supported by data, research, and consensus. Statements of significance describe the distinctive nature of the park and why an area is important within a global, national, regional, and systemwide context. They focus on the most important resources and values that will assist in park planning and management. The following significance statements have been identified for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park. (Please note that the sequence of the statements does not reflect the level of significance.) 1. The US Supreme Court consolidated five cases from four states and the District of Columbia and decided the cases in two decisions on the same day in 1954. The court declared unanimously that the doctrine of “separate but equal,” established in the court’s 1896 decision in Plessy v. Ferguson, no longer applied in the realm of public education. The decisions interpreted clearly the constitutional right of all persons to equal protection of the law as guaranteed by the 14th and 5th amendments to the US Constitution. The decisions, commonly referred together to as the Brown v. Board of Education decision, established a legal precedent that led to the dismantling of other forms of segregation in the country during the height of the modern civil rights movement in the 1950s and 1960s. 2. The five cases—Briggs v. Elliott, Bolling v. Sharpe, Brown v. Board of Education, Davis v. County School Board, and Gebhart v. Belton—consolidated as Brown v. Board of Education, reflect regional dynamics, showing how systemic racial segregation impacted education across diverse geographic locations in the United States. Each case—originating from South Carolina, Washington, DC, Kansas, Virginia, and Delaware—highlights unique local circumstances that nonetheless underscore a shared national struggle against segregated schooling. 3. Attorneys from the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People (NAACP) chose cases that proved crucial to the Supreme Court’s decision in Brown v. Board of Education. The case Briggs v. Elliott from deeply unequal Clarendon County, South Carolina, compelled the state to advance an “equalization” strategy that would comply with the Plessy doctrine by closing the disparity between Black and White school facilities. Scott’s Branch High School was one of the first “equalization schools” built in the early 1950s. At the other extreme, segregated elementary schools for Blacks in Topeka, Kansas, including Monroe School, were tangibly equal facilities that provided equal—or better—education to Black pupils. Yet, expert testimony from social scientists urged the court to move beyond measuring purely financial or physical inequalities to conclude that legalized and forced segregation itself had negative psychological effects on African American children and, therefore, should not be allowed. 4. The struggle for education equity has a long history in the United States. Many communities and excluded groups have contributed to that history. The sites included in Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park represent the perseverance and activism of community members—especially young people and their parents—as advocates for education equity. These communities symbolically represent the many other places and cases that built a history of judicial decisions stretching back into the 1800s and moving forward from Brown in legal and political efforts to achieve education equity. They also demonstrate the spectrum of reactions to the Brown decisions, from compliance to various forms of massive resistance. 5. Beyond the immediate effects the Brown decision had on segregated schools, the impact of the decision provided the legal principle—“segregation is inherently unequal”—that created a legacy for future movements to work on dismantling societal inequities. The decision also has had a broad global impact and has often been cited in other nations’ courts to establish a fundamental human value of racial equality and the right to an education. Fundamental Resources and Values Fundamental resources and values (FRVs) are those features, systems, processes, experiences, stories, scenes, sounds, smells, or other attributes determined to warrant primary consideration during planning and management processes because they are essential to achieving the purpose of the park and maintaining its significance. Fundamental resources and values are closely related to a park’s legislative purpose and are more specific than significance statements. Fundamental resources and values help focus planning and management efforts on what is truly significant about the park. One of the most important responsibilities of NPS managers is to ensure the conservation and public enjoyment of those qualities that are essential (fundamental) to achieving the purpose of the park and maintaining its significance. If fundamental resources and values are allowed to deteriorate, the park purpose and/or significance could be jeopardized. The following fundamental resources and values have been identified for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park: · Monroe Elementary School and Grounds. As one of four segregated elementary schools for Black children, Monroe is an example of the quality of education provided to African Americans in comparison to White pupils in Topeka’s elementary schools. By any measure at the time, the quality of education provided to Black children in segregated elementary schools was equal to—or better than—that provided to White children. By traditional interpretations of the Constitution, therefore, Topeka was “separate but equal.” The Supreme Court crucially ruled that despite the comparable availability of funding and facilities for Black and White students, “separate is inherently unequal.” The two-story brick building and surrounding grounds retain their appearance from the time of the court case. The building serves as the Topeka Visitor Center as well as park headquarters. · Scott’s Branch High School and Summerton High School. The disparity between the wood frame Scott’s Branch School and the brick Summerton High School, both built in the mid-1930s, was at issue in the Briggs v. Elliott case. During 1951, in an effort to make schools truly “separate but equal,” the state attempted to “equalize” school facilities for Black and White children by constructing a brick and cinderblock facility for Black children adjacent to their existing wood frame school. The wood frame structure was eventually demolished, but the brick and cinderblock Scott’s Branch school still stands today. Summerton High School was the better-resourced school for White students and was eventually integrated after the Brown decision. Both surviving buildings retain a substantial amount of their historical integrity to the time of the Briggs case and immediately after. · Oral Histories. Recording eyewitness accounts of participants in the Brown v. Board of Education cases has been an important method to “honor the civil rights stories of struggle, perseverance, and activism in the pursuit of education equity” as directed in the park’s enabling legislation. As older generations give way to newer ones, the park will continue to collect and preserve oral history interviews as valuable assets for understanding the impacts of the Brown cases and the obstacles to achieving education equity. Other Important Resources and Values Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park contains other resources and values that are not fundamental to the purpose of the park and may be unrelated to its significance but are important to consider in planning processes. These are referred to as “other important resources and values” (OIRV). These resources and values have been selected because they are important in the operation and management of the park and warrant special consideration in park planning. The following other important resources and values have been identified for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park: · Associations/Partnerships. The park’s enabling and expansion legislation directs the National Park Service to interpret the impact of the Brown v. Board of Education decisions on civil rights history in the US and to assist in the preservation, protection, and interpretation of the Brown-related sites in DC and four states. In order to achieve these directives, the park relies on partnerships with the owners of the affiliated areas and with museums, colleges and universities, heritage tourism agencies, and other nonprofit organizations. · Archeological Collections. The park’s archeological collections consist of artifacts reflecting the lives and material culture of those who lived and learned on the land. The archeological resources, combined with historical information, tell the story of migration and settlement. For example, artifacts relating to residents who lived in the Monroe Elementary School neighborhood from the late 1860s until 1928 reflect those who lived during the segregation era and were the ancestors of those who ultimately pushed for equality in the 1950s and 1960s. Future investigations in Summerton will likely reveal similar artifacts that illuminate the history of education in the community. The park’s archeological collections warrant special consideration as park resources. Interpretive Themes Interpretive themes are often described as the key stories or concepts that visitors should understand after visiting a park—they define the most important ideas or concepts communicated to visitors about a park unit. Themes are derived from, and should reflect, park purpose, significance, resources, and values. The set of interpretive themes is complete when it provides the structure necessary for park staff to develop opportunities for visitors to explore and relate to all park significance statements and fundamental and other important resources and values. Interpretive themes are an organizational tool that reveal and clarify meaning, concepts, contexts, and values represented by park resources. Sound themes are accurate and reflect current scholarship and science. They encourage exploration of the context in which events or natural processes occurred and the effects of those events and processes. Interpretive themes go beyond a mere description of the event or process to foster multiple opportunities to experience and consider the park and its resources. These themes help explain why a park story is relevant to people who may otherwise be unaware of connections they have to an event, time, or place associated with the park. The following interpretive themes have been identified for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park: · A century of personal struggles, community activism, and legal battles culminated in the US Supreme Court’s decisions in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954. This theme explores the legal, political, moral, and social circumstances leading up to the cases and the cases themselves as representative of many other struggles in the US for educational equality and civil rights. · The local communities that initiated the five court cases comprising Brown v. Board of Education represented a broad range of economic, geographic, and cultural contexts, ranging from rural areas to thriving cities. Many people risked their safety and livelihoods to advocate for change in the face of massive resistance, and they suffered significant consequences as a result of the legal decisions. This theme conveys the significance of the “case of the century” as the result of the efforts of many people in diverse places over a long time, to honor their civil rights stories of struggle, activism, and perseverance, and to inspire audiences through those stories of personal sacrifices made for the greater common good. · The Brown v. Board of Education decisions provide the foundation for the major civil rights actions taken by the executive, judicial, and legislative branches of government and by more and more citizens, as the struggles broadened to include other groups in American society, establishing a landmark precedent that continues to inspire debate over the meanings of equality to the present day. This theme delves into the subsequent impact of the Supreme Court’s decisions in the struggle for education equity and in the many other legacies of the decisions. It is intended to convey the complex, interconnected nature of constitutional rights across groups and generations. · The Brown v. Board of Education decisions have informed the international movement for civil and human rights. National courts in many countries have used the Brown v. Board of Education decisions in their own opinions that have expanded rights and freedoms across the world. This theme highlights the international impact of the US Supreme Court’s decisions and conveys the far-reaching significance of those decisions in the context of global history. · The broad story of Brown v. Board of Education in the context of the American civil rights movement inspires the celebration of our common humanity and reminds us that engaged citizens through collective action, whether they are students, parents, teachers, lawyers, or judges, can propel a nation—and the world—toward equality and justice for all. This theme emphasizes democratic engagement. Special Mandates Special mandates are requirements specific to a park that must be fulfilled. Mandates can be expressed in enabling legislation, in separate legislation following the establishment of the park, or through a judicial process. They may expand on park purpose or introduce elements unrelated to the purpose of the park. They are an essential component of managing and planning for Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park. · Property Acquisition. The park’s enabling legislation as amended mandates and places conditions on property acquisition, including that any property owned by the states of Kansas or South Carolina or any political subdivision thereof may be acquired only by donation. The secretary of the interior may also acquire personal property associated with, and appropriate for, the interpretation of the historical park. The secretary may not acquire such personal property without the consent of the owner or by condemnation of any land or interest in land within the boundaries of the historical park. · Cooperative Agreements. The park’s enabling legislation as amended authorizes the secretary of the interior to enter into cooperative agreements with private as well as public agencies, organizations, and institutions in furtherance of the purposes of the enabling legislation as amended. · Affiliated Areas. The park’s enabling legislation as amended identifies five “affiliated areas” for their association with a court case included in Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka. The NPS may provide technical and financial assistance to, and enter into cooperative agreements with, the management entity for each affiliated area to provide financial assistance for the marketing, marking, interpretation, and preservation of the applicable affiliated area. A decision memorandum signed by the secretary of the interior on January 9, 2025, established the five sites associated with Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park as affiliated areas of the national park system: 1) The Robert Russa Moton Museum in Farmville, Virginia; 2) the former Howard High School in Wilmington, Delaware; 3) Claymont High School in Claymont, Delaware; 4) Hockessin Colored School #107 in Hockessin, Delaware; and 5) John Philip Sousa Middle School in the District of Columbia. (See additional information in “Affiliated Areas” below). Affiliated Areas As noted in Special Mandates above, legislation redesignating and expanding Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park also legislated affiliated areas. While the five affiliated areas are not managed by the NPS, they are eligible for NPS technical and financial assistance and are required to be managed in accordance with laws generally applicable to sites in the National Park System. A decision memorandum signed by the secretary of the interior on January 9, 2025, affirms that the conditions of the legislation have been met by each affiliated area. These areas are required to be managed in a manner consistent with laws generally applicable to units of the National Park System and in accordance with NPS Policy Memorandum 24-04 on Affiliated Areas, which was issued by the NPS Director on October 15, 2024. Public Law 117-123 states that cooperative agreements between the NPS and each management entity are necessary for providing technical and financial assistance for the marketing, marking, interpretation, and preservation of each affiliated area. Policy Memorandum 24-04 confirms the essential role of agreements between the NPS and a management entity. The park’s enabling legislation as amended also requires that the NPS, in consultation with the management entity, develop a management plan for each area. The legislation includes further stipulations about the management plan and public comment (See Appendix A). Robert Russa Moton Museum (Farmville, Virginia) Built in 1939, the Robert Russa Moton High School was the African American high school for Prince Edward County, Virginia. The one-story red brick building remains virtually unchanged from the original design. In 1951, students from the school began a strike that proved to be critical in the march towards challenging “separate but equal.” The strike led to Davis v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, a case decided in the Brown v. Board of Education decisions. Davis was the only student-initiated case of the five that comprised Brown v. Board of Education. Though the Brown decision held that segregation was unconstitutional, Virginians joined the “massive resistance” of other southern states. Though other school districts in Virginia closed schools for days or weeks, Prince Edward County was the only county in the nation to close its schools for five years, between 1959 and 1964, rather than desegregate. In Griffin v. County School Board of Prince Edward County, the Supreme Court intervened again to reopen the schools. The school building is a National Historic Landmark, a property recognized as having exceptional value or quality in illustrating or interpreting the heritage of the United States. Since 2001, it has housed the Robert Russa Moton Museum, which preserves and constructively interprets how Prince Edward County relates to the history of civil rights in education and the leading role its citizens played in America’s transition from segregation toward integration. The museum strives to promote dialogue and advance positions that ensure empowerment within a constitutional democracy. In 2015, the museum and Longwood University entered into a perpetual agreement including a commitment by both institutions to work together to ensure “that the Museum as a landmark site is regularly open to the general public, in order to further its mission of advancing civil rights in education.” Management Entity: The Board of Trustees of the Robert Russa Moton Museum, Inc. Howard High School (Wilmington, Delaware) Built in 1927, the former Howard High School is located in the urban setting of Wilmington, Delaware. The roots of the school date back to 1867, and for many decades, the school was the only secondary school available to African American youth in the entire state of Delaware. As evidenced by photographs taken when the school opened, the interior maintains much of its historical identity. The library is now maintained by the Afro-American Historical Society of Delaware and the Howard Alumni Association to store reference materials and other memorabilia. A group of parents at Howard requested the school board allow their children to attend the all-White Claymont High School because it was within a shorter walking distance of their homes than Howard High. The school board denied this request. The parents took legal action which evolved into Belton v. Gebhart, one of the cases combined to form Brown v. Board of Education. Now known as Howard High School of Technology, the building retains much of its historical integrity and is now a National Historic Landmark. It was chosen as one of the representative buildings in Delaware to be an affiliated area of Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park. Howard High School also has an active alumni association. Claymont High School (Claymont, Delaware) Claymont High School, constructed between 1924 and 1925, was the subject of the Belton v. Gebhart case. The White-only school was also known as the Green Street School. In 1951, when Black students were denied admission, their case went to the Delaware Chancery Court. After the state court ruling in 1952, Black students were successfully enrolled. The ruling was limited in that it did not apply to schools statewide. Claymont was the first public high school in the 17 segregated states to be legally integrated. From there, the community became part of the Brown v. Board of Education case before the US Supreme Court. In 1980, the building became the home of the Claymont Community Center and was administered by the Brandywine Community Resource Council, Inc. The center operates a rich variety of programs today to support its mission to “enhance the community by addressing the human needs of wellness, belongingness and esteem.” Management Entity: Brandywine Community Resource Council, Inc., Board of Directors. Hockessin Colored School #107 (Hockessin, Delaware) Hockessin School #107C, the subject of the Bulah v. Gebhart case, was a “colored” elementary school that students were required to attend without any available transportation. Both the Bulah and Belton cases argued that the facilities and transportation options for Black children were not equal to those for White children. While filed separately in the Delaware courts, the cases eventually were combined. The chancery court decision concluded in both cases that the plaintiffs were in fact correct: the facilities were substantially unequal. They ordered injunctions barring the defendants from denying admission to the plaintiffs. The school is now used as a community facility by Friends of Hockessin Colored School #107, Inc. (FOHCS), a nonprofit corporation in the State of Delaware who saved the school from a sheriff’s sale and has since raised the funds necessary to renovate the school, install museum exhibits, and operate “a Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Social Equity.” FOHCS entered into a partnership agreement with New Castle County in August 2020 to become a county park with the purpose of insuring that “the FOHCS mission would be financially sustainable in perpetuity.” Management Entity: The Friends of Hockessin Colored School #107, Inc. John Philip Sousa Middle School (Washington, District of Columbia) Built in 1950 in Southeast Washington, DC, and formerly known as John Philip Sousa Junior High School, the Sousa Middle School was the site of an attempt at school integration. When Black students were denied admission to the all-White school, the Bolling v. Sharpe case was filed by James Nabrit Jr., a professor at Howard University School of Law. The New Deal program in the 1930s offered Black Americans their first chance to secure government jobs, uniquely suiting Washington for rapid growth in the Black population. This influx of families led to overcrowding in Black schools, the buildings often holding double or even triple the amount suggested for them. In a story similar to those of the other affiliated-area schools, a group of determined parents relentlessly argued for better circumstances for their children. The culmination was the inclusion of Bolling v. Sharpe in the combined Brown v. Board of Education cases argued in front of the US Supreme Court in 1954. Today, the school remains a National Historic Landmark. The building is still in use as a public school, operated by the District of Columbia Public Schools, which itself is administered by the District of Columbia General Services Administration. Related Resources Related resources are not owned by the National Park Service. They may be part of the broader context or setting in which park resources exist, represent a thematic connection that would enhance the experience of visitors, or have close associations with park fundamental resources and the purpose of the park. The related resources represent a connection with the park that often reflects an area of mutual benefit or interest, and collaboration, between the park and owner/stakeholder. Resources listed as related are those directly related to the court cases in each of the five communities, as well as a list of major repositories of oral histories and archival collections. A comprehensive list of resources related to predecessor cases and the people involved is beyond the scope of a foundation document. The related resources here have typically been recognized for their role in the Brown cases and decisions by being placed on the National Register of Historic Places, declared a National Historic Landmark, or recognized in some other way by the federal government or state historic preservation offices. The following resources related to Brown v. Board of Education National Historical Park are grouped by location: South Carolina · Liberty Hill AME Church: Throughout the 1940s and 1950s, the church hosted meetings of African American students and parents in Summerton. In 1955, the church welcomed Thurgood Marshall to a meeting about school desegregation. · St. Mark AME Church: The church often served as a place for the NAACP to meet with African American students and parents in Summerton, including the petitioners in the Briggs v. Elliott lawsuit. · Harry and Eliza Briggs Home: The Briggs family welcomed community members into their home to sign the petition that became Briggs v. Elliott. They and others faced severe retribution after the Brown decisions and only returned from out of state in 1976. · Center for Civil Rights History and Research, University of South Carolina: The center provides educational programming and public engagement about Briggs v. Elliott and houses the papers of the Reverend Joseph A. De Laine. · Cecil Williams South Carolina Civil Rights Museum: Located in Orangeburg, the museum curates the largest collection of artifacts related to the people at the center of Briggs v. Elliott. Kansas · Sumner Elementary School: A National Historic Landmark, Sumner is identified in the park’s enabling legislation as worthy of NPS protection as an example of the White elementary schools that Black children were prevented from attending. · Historic US Post Office and Court House: The district court heard and decided the case of Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka here. The building is listed in the National Register of Historic Places. · Lucinda Todd Home: Plaintiff Lucinda Todd helped operate the Citizens Committee on Civil Rights from here. As secretary of the Topeka Chapter of the NAACP, Todd used her home as a hub of activity in what became the Brown v. Board of Education of Topeka lawsuit. The home is listed in the National Register of Historic Places. · Kansas Historical Society: Archival collections include the Brown v. Topeka Board of Education Oral History Collection and many manuscripts related to the Brown cases—not just the Kansas case. Delaware · Delaware Public Archives: Houses the court, attorney general, and governor papers related to the Delaware cases and the aftermath of the Brown decisions. Virginia · Longwood University: The Greenwood Library Archives and Special Collections include oral histories of civil rights in Prince Edward County and manuscripts related to the Davis v. Prince Edward County case and the closure of schools in the county. District of Columbia · Charles Sumner School Museum and Archives: The official museum and archives of public education in the District of Columbia with emphasis upon the instruction of African American students. · National Archives Building: The main archives hold the records of the District Court of DC (Bolling v. Sharpe) and the records of the US Supreme Court. National Archives Regional Locations · District Court records are located in Atlanta (Briggs v. Elliott), Kansas City (Brown v. Board of Education), and Philadelphia (Davis v. Prince Edward County). · Records of executive agencies related to the Brown decisions are housed at the National Archives in College Park, Maryland. Records of the Office of the President are found at the respective presidential libraries. Contributors Brown v.
